nature-pol-011.title: The global waste trade: shipping rubbish across borders
nature-pol-011.text: Waste mostly flows from the Global North to be disposed of in the Global South. The global waste trade ships it between countries for treatment, disposal or {{ref:nature-eecon-038}}. Richer, more urbanized countries produce more solid waste, and developing countries often import toxic or hazardous waste from developed ones. Scholars link the trade's sharp growth to the free-market policies of the 1980s, which pushed developing countries to import waste as a route to economic expansion. Supporters argue it can stimulate economies with little else to offer the global economy. Critics see dumping. Most hazardous waste is produced in the United States and Europe, yet the health harms fall on poorer countries. Lacking safe facilities, people there handle toxic waste by hand, and poor disposal causes illness and death. Dump sites carry heavy metals and persistent organic pollutants that kill birds, fish and other wildlife. The trade is hard to regulate, since vague definitions let hazardous waste be exported as commodities or raw materials.

nature-pol-006.title: The pollution haven hypothesis: do dirty industries flee strict rules?
nature-pol-006.text: After the US tightened lead air standards in 2009, exports of used lead-acid batteries to Mexico rose four-fold. More low-birth-weight babies followed near Mexican plants that reprocess them. The pollution haven hypothesis holds that firms investing abroad move to countries with cheap resources and weak environmental rules, making them havens for pollution. The logic is cost. Stricter rules raise input costs for pollution-intensive goods and erode a place's {{ref:nature-econ-106}}. The claim comes in three strengths: pollution costs matter at the margin; they measurably shift trade and investment; or countries deliberately set standards too low to attract investment. The first two have empirical support. How much the effect matters next to other trade and investment factors remains disputed. It may partly explain the {{ref:nature-eecon-225}}, as polluting industry shifts from richer to poorer economies.

nature-pol-014.title: The e-waste trade: rich countries' old electronics
nature-pol-014.text: An estimated 50 million tons of e-waste are produced each year, mostly in the United States and Europe. Most is shipped to Asia and Africa for processing and {{ref:nature-eecon-038}}. The trade grows with fast technological change, falling prices and {{ref:nature-eecon-188}}. Heavy metals and toxins leak into waterways and underground water. They expose dump workers, children searching for items to sell and nearby residents. In Guiyu, China, possibly the world's largest e-waste dump, workers dismantle over 1.5 million pounds of junked electronics a year.

nature-pol-013.title: Toxic colonialism: poorer countries as dumping grounds
nature-pol-013.text: Toxic colonialism is the use of poorer countries as cheap places to export or dump the hazardous waste of developed countries. It is the core critique of the global waste trade. The word 'colonialism' fits, critics say, because economic dependence, exploitation of labor and cultural inequality mark both. T.V. Reed links it to colonial views of indigenous land as empty 'waste', which make Global South land seem expendable for Western wastes. Laura Pratt argues agreements have not stopped it, because waste moves under false permits, bribes, improper labels or the pretext of reuse.

nature-pol-010.title: Has the WTO delivered? The critics' case
nature-pol-010.text: Ha-Joon Chang notes that developing countries grew faster in 1960–1980 than in 1980–2000, even though their trade policies are now far more liberal. Critics say the gains from WTO-backed free trade are not shared equally, pointing to widening gaps between rich and poor. They fear early liberalizing traps developing economies in the primary sector, which often needs little skilled labor. Vietnam cut poverty and grew fast while liberalizing slowly with safeguards; El Salvador's growth stayed weak after it removed import barriers and cut tariffs. Studies credit the WTO with boosting trade, but whether liberalizing reliably brings growth and less hardship remains disputed.

nature-pol-017.title: The Bamako Convention: Africa bans imported hazardous waste
nature-pol-017.text: In 1991 African nations, unhappy with the {{ref:nature-gov-129}}, signed the Bamako Convention. It goes further, banning imports of all hazardous waste generated outside the Organization of African Unity and treating imports from non-parties as illegal. Its reach was very limited, though. With scarce resources and weak enforcement, members could not stop toxic dumping. The Lomé IV Convention similarly banned exports of hazardous wastes from the European Community to African, Caribbean and Pacific states.

nature-pol-012.title: The economic case for exporting waste
nature-pol-012.text: In a 1991 memo, Lawrence Summers, then World Bank chief economist, wrote that the economic logic of dumping toxic waste in the lowest-wage country was 'impeccable'. The memo called countries in Africa 'vastly under polluted'. It asked whether the World Bank should encourage dirty industries to move to the least developed countries. A Cato Institute article argued that people in developing countries would rationally accept more exposure to pollutants for higher productivity and income. The case rests mainly on their need for economic development. Critics call the practice {{ref:nature-pol-013}}.

nature-pol-042.title: Rent-seeking: getting richer without creating wealth
nature-pol-042.text: Robert Shiller's classic example is a landowner who chains a river and charges passing boats to lower the chain. The landowner adds no value. That is rent-seeking. It means growing richer by manipulating public policy or economic conditions, without creating new wealth. Here 'rent' means {{ref:nature-res-218}}: income beyond what is needed to keep a factor in its current use. Profit-seeking creates wealth through mutually beneficial trade; rent-seeking only redistributes existing wealth. Typical examples are lobbying for subsidies, tariffs, quotas or rules that hobble competitors. The costs are broad. Rent-seeking wastes resources, stifles competition, lowers wealth creation and government revenue, and raises inequality and corruption risk. Money spent on lobbyists rather than research or equipment slows growth, and Mancur Olson argued that countries dominated by organized interest groups lose vitality and decline. Critics note it can be hard to tell beneficial profit-seeking from harmful rent-seeking.

nature-pol-198.title: Counting fossil fuel subsidies: why the totals differ
nature-pol-198.text: In 2021 the UK government said it did not subsidize fossil fuels under the IEA definition, while others said it did under the OECD definition. Estimates add up payments, compare prices with world prices, and may count health and climate damage. Counting unpriced damage makes IMF estimates far larger than those using OECD and International Energy Agency definitions. One IMF paper found underpricing of local air pollution was the largest part of global subsidies, at 42%, followed by global warming costs at 29%. The fiscal cost of government support for fossil fuels was 1.1 trillion USD in 2023, 90% of it tied to consumption.
